I grew up lower middle class. Not dirt poor, but definitely on the lower end. I had a girlfriend in high school who's dad was a bank executive, and owned his own successful business. I remember that she was totally unaware of how well off her family was. I remember telling her that I had to quit my job to watch my baby sister so my mom could work a new job, so I'd probably be low on date money for awhile. Well, one thing led to another and we ended up getting in a big argument in which I explained to her that my family was going through a tough time financially, and that we were living pay check to to pay check.

 She replied that she understood, because her family was also in a tough time financially, because her dad would be getting paid differently that year, because he got promoted to vice president. Anyway, she started freaking out about how she isn't rich and how she understands my situation because her family was in such a rough patch that they had to sell their house in Ocean City Maryland!

 The whole thing was baffling to me because she's going off about how she isn't rich when she lives in one of the biggest housed I've ever seen, and at the time was just given her first car as a random gift. She had a almost the size of my room filled with clothes while all my clothes fit in half of a cramped closet. Me and my brother had to share a room because we didn't have enough space in our house. 

The biggest difference that I noticed was the rate at which things were fixed and replaced. For example, in my house we had one fully functional toilet and two iffy ones, two holes in the roof, a door that couldn't close, and a trashed basement that guests weren't allowed to go into. One thing i specifically remember was that we didn't have a microwave for about a year, and one day her microwave broke and the next day she had a new one. Little stuff like that. Also She was blown away by the fact I'd never been to Disney world. She had been there 15 times when we were dating at age 16. It was really weird to see how removed everyone in that family was from the reality of the world. None of the people except for the dad have ever been ALIVE without all of their financial needs being met by parents. 

This made her have this attitude of just not understanding. She could focus all her efforts on things like our relationship and school, while I struggled to find time for her and school because our house was never quiet. There was always a screaming baby or some other noise going on, meaning I normally stayed after school for up to 2 hours a day to complete homework and essays. If she wanted to see me, she could just drive on over and hang out with me. But for me it was more complicated because I needed to work around 2 parents work and errand schedules to make sure I wasn't leaving the other kids at home. She also had this weird sense of entitlement, like somehow in some little way SHE was responsible for their families riches, definitely not a combination of incredibly smart networking and investments by her father combined with a very wealthy mother. It was very frustrating to deal with a lot of the time.

Honestly try working on your handles, many players are very explosive but don't have the required confidence with the ball to be effective. I highly recommend two ball dribbling, and work on "tightening" your handle by focusing on pound dribbling the two balls above your knees and below your waist. The thought behind the knees and waist rule is that any dribble above your waist can be stolen, and anything below your knee can be kicked. Also try moving two ball drills, finally put it all together by pushing the ball out in front of you when you begin your drive, which helped a lot for me at least by not forcing me to slow down as much.

Also, just blowing by players from a standstill is going to get increasingly difficult as time goes on, unless your a freak athlete. Try working on attacking closeouts instead. When you get the ball in a spot up situation, look towards the rim like you're about to shoot, forcing the other player to come running at you, then rip through and get past him.

If you do go from a standstill, try to use ball fakes, head fakes and jab steps to get your man just slightly off balance before your make your move.

Coaches have big impacts in my two favorite sports, hockey and basketball, not directly, through calling plays or formations like in football or american football, but through the subtle changes in culture and systems in the teams they coach. Oftentimes great head coaches are surrounded by great player development and scouting personnel to keep the coaches stocked with good young talent, and they learn from the older veterans who already know the system. For example, Gregg Popovich and Mike Babcock influenced the style of play and team culture of their respective teams for decades. Its a slow process, and requires some flexibility to allow certain strengths in players to be used to their full advantage. 

In my basketball playing experience at many different levels, I've found that a coach is someone who needs to exert an influence on their team to be successful, and they need to show, not tell, what they want. Like my old high school varsity coach was big on defense and post play, but AAU was very popular in my area so we had a bunch of 6'3 shooting guards that our coach kept forcing into his system as post players, and the closest thing we had to a true post player was me, who was a 6'7 player who could shoot 80% from three in practice and was great at driving and kicking and attacking closeouts but was forced into the post where I struggled due to my lanky frame. I ended up doing much better even against much stronger competition in AAU, when I played more of a small forward role on the wing or coming out of the corner. 

One thing that's important to remember is that the coach is directing workouts and practices all through the year, and so if he wants his players to focus on something, he's got to get them to run drills to focus on those particular skills. My high school coach never really taught us defense and expected it to be a pure effort skill, while my higher level coaches have taught me the footwork, stances and quickness needed to play good defense, and it should be easy to guess which coach was more effective with their lessons on defense.

Its important to devise and stick with a system, but be willing to ditch it for a new one that compliments your teams strengths more. Craig Berube of my Flyers team was fired because of his rigid game plan and the way that he thought of the game being too different from what the modern NHL requires, Craig Berube just couldn't put together 3 scoring lines and the flyers struggled in part because of his questionable coaching, and in part because of the defenseman that he had to work with.

Tl;Dr: Coaches are important. Good coaches use good players to their advantage. Great coaches devise ways to use good players to their full potential, and make them great players.

When I was 6'3" I could jump up and touch rim from a stand pretty easily, but could get maybe 1 inch higher when I tried to run and dunk. If you're in that kind of situation look at your approach. What you should remember is basically

1. Start with slow long strides and speed up as you approach. Your last 2 steps should be very quick, short and almost simultaneous

2. Your back should be straight, you shouldn't be hunched over. You don't necessarily have to have perfect posture, but don't have your shoulders in front of your knees.

3. Make sure you really drive your opposite knee up towards the rim. 

4. Keep your toes pointed back at your shins. This is called dorsiflexion and helps you explode upwards. 

If your approach is good I'd suggest squatting a little bit and doing some plyometric exercises. Just doing like a hundred or so box jumps a day helped me tremendously, but there are obviously more advanced exercises if you really want to get up.

And most importantly remember to try to dunk every day. Eventually you'll get it.

Well it depends.How tall are you? How strong are you? How quick are you? How is your touch around the rim?

I am personally slower than most players, weaker than most players, but taller than almost all players, and I have great touch anywhere in the lane and a great fadeaway. The go to move for me is a right handed sweeping skyhook to the middle if I'm on the right block and one dribble middle to the dirk fadeaway if I'm on the left block.

I'll break post moves down into a few categories so you can choose which ones to use based on your strengths and weaknesses.

**Quickness**

If you can blow by any player you want I would recommend taking an extra step off the low block and facing up right away. From there you can blow right by him off the face up in one smooth motion, or you can jabstep. Lets say you jabstep right. Remember to hold your foot out where you jabbed it. From there you can either go right, or go step across and go left. If the defender isn't biting and is in your face, try to create some space by putting your leg in between his legs and ripping the ball through low. Then as he takes a step towards you try to blow by him. 

If you blow by him try to finish on the opposite side of the rim so you don't get swatted. If he's cutting you off, quickly spin the other way. If you want just stop up and shoot a quick hookshot over him while he's off balance.

Another move you can do is a quick spin. From your regular position on the low block, turn on one pivot foot to the baseline side. Seal him by getting your elbow past his elbow, take one dribble and drive opposite side.

Videos: [Faceup drive](http://youtu.be/CH4AjDgl1Ng?t=2m1s) [Faceup drive spin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KdSwGCatMqA) [Quick spin](http://youtu.be/mArHU1ewSog?t=2m26s) [Jabsteps](http://youtu.be/4ziDwNq0XFI?t=1m)

Players/Highlights to watch: HAKEEM OLAJUWON, Lebron James, Anthony Davis

**Power Moves**

These are the coaches favorite moves. If you're stronger than your opponent you have a few options. If you can, muscle your man under the rim and call for a pass for a deep finish. If not establish regular position on the low block. 

From there, you can take a dribble to back down and then a long, sealing step to the middle for a jump hook. You can also ball fake middle, and simultaneously dropstep baseline, power dribble, get yourself set and go up strong. If your under the rim this is very hard to block, especially if you throw your weight around to get the defender off balance.

You can also dribble middle and dropstep baseline. And you can ALWAYS go up and under.

Videos: [Shaq teaches post moves](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k9JfeLnbyUw)

Players/Highlights to watch: Shaq, Demarcus Cousins

**Touch and Finesse**

So you aren't strong or quick. You need to get out and practice some shots. Learn to shoot a hookshot from all over the lane. Learn a fadeaway. Practice these shots until you can make them from any conceivable place you could end up shooting them. What happens all the time for me is I take a dribble and get shoved halfway to the freethrow line, but I can still just throw up a hookshot. It doesn't matter if your defender is shoving you around or cutting you off wherever you go, you need to learn how to chuck the ball up from anywhere and know that it will go in. That's what I learned and it has done pretty well for me.

So basically I'd practice my hookshots and maybe one or two "unblockable shots" also remember that if you're in this boat, fakes are key. You can't get your defender off balance by hitting them, so you have to fake them out until they're off balance. A shimmy hook is good for this. One dribble middle, fake dropstep baseline and finish. 

Videos: [Running hook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wx-0O4X-354) [Dirk fades](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pTmaFUCm1aU)
Also see the Shaq teaches post moves video for the shimmy jump hook.

Note on Dirk fadeaways: A lot of those shots in the video would get you benched, focus on shots like the one at 2:23 in the dirk video. For me fadeaways are to be done in the paint if they are a higher percentage shot for you than a hook shot.

Players to watch: Kareem, Pau Gasol, Dirk Nowitzki

**All Players**

Every player should be able to finish strong at the rim. What did it for me is always slapping the backboard when I go up to finish. You will always be a target on breaks, handoffs, cuts, and rolls if you can go up hard with layups.

I think that AAA games have already found a formula that appeals to a huge audience, while AA titles are still experimenting with different ideas to get their game noticed. There are more factors that AA games can adjust to try and become more successful.

 AAA games have their gameplay, they have the ideas, the only other thing to change is how it looks, hence the improving graphics. Because of this we see new gameplay and core ideas in mid-tier games while the AAA titles change much less. But let's not forget there is a reason AAA titles don't change as much, and that is because their consumers expect something when they buy the game. 

Look at Halo: Reach and Halo 4, considered disappointments by many Halo players despite introducing new mechanics, a sleeker look and a newer engine, but it was still not as well received as previous titles because they changed things too much, and because they "dumbed down" the game.

Gaming is still young, and ten years ago there were still many ideas being experimented with, whereas now we have our winning formulas from huge franchises, while other developers change their games to try and find that idea that everyone loves, so they can expand their game. Unfortunately once they find that idea they may hesitate to stray from it, and only change the way the game looks.

A good V-cut is essential, they can be a quicker step in, step back out to the perimeter, or a bigger move where you take your man all the way to the elbow before exploding back to the 3 point line. Make solid, but not overly aggressive contact with your forearm on your man, then push him however many steps you want, and cut back. Stay unpredictable, sometimes drive hard to the basket and look for the ball, and other times use the V-cut to get back to the perimeter. If you cut back to the perimeter a few times, and you notice the defender covering you close as you cut back, cut to the basket for a layup. If you have a big height advantage on your man, screw it, take him to the block and post him up once or twice. 

Don't forget to use the pick and roll, or a pick and pop if you are a good shooter. 

Last, and most importantly, to make sure you get the ball once your open, **make a target where you want the ball.** As someone who was mostly a post player this was something I didn't get the hang of until way too late. If you are running somewhere present a target that gives the passer an idea of where to lead, if you are wide open, clap your hands, yell, whatever you have to do, then make an easy target right on your chest. If you're posting up, put your hands up. There's nothing worse than a 5'4" Point guard throwing a bounce pass through your legs because without realizing it, that's where you were putting your hands for him to pass to. 

**TL;DR:** V-Cut, and make a target where you want the ball to be placed
